transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Um... well, I guess it's just that people are starting to notice that I can't really sit and listen. I keep getting up when I'm supposed to stay put. It happens during client interviews, or... tutoring sessions. Even at book club. So... yeah, that's what brings me in.
When did you first notice this difficulty sitting still and staying focused? Has this been happening your whole life, or is it something newer?

Um... I suppose it's not new. It's been my whole life, really. 

I mean... if you look at my old grade-school report cards, they always said I was bright, but... that I couldn't stay in my seat. Or wait my turn. My mother actually still jokes about it. She says I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through. 

So... yeah. It's always been there.
Besides the difficulty sitting still, do you also find it hard to concentrate or focus on tasks—like when you're reading, working on a project, or listening to someone speak?
Um... no, not really. I don't think I have a problem with that. I can focus on things fine... it's just the staying in one place that's the issue.

Do you find yourself doing things without thinking them through first, or acting on impulse? For example, interrupting people, making snap decisions, or doing things without considering the consequences?

Um... I guess the interrupting part, yeah. Like... if I overhear the junior detectives at work discussing a lead, or... even just neighbors talking in the hallway. I tend to just jump in. Ask questions or give advice before anyone asks me. 

And... well, afterward I realize I completely barged into someone else's conversation. So... I suppose I do that.

You mentioned having trouble sitting still at work and in social situations. Do you also notice this restlessness or need to move around when you're doing things on your own, like at home relaxing or working on a personal project?

Um... yeah, I suppose so. Even on days when I don't have field work... I don't really stop. I just move from unpacking boxes to... reorganizing case files, or running errands. It's... well, it's like I'm still chasing a lead. I just have a hard time actually being off duty.
When you look back at your childhood, do you remember these issues with sitting still and interrupting others starting before you were around 12 years old?

Um... yeah, I suppose so. I mean, my mother still brings it up. She jokes that I treated every classroom like... a crime scene I had to pace through. And... I guess my old report cards from grade school usually said something similar. That I was bright, but... couldn't stay in my seat. Or wait my turn. So, yes... it's been a while.
How much is this restlessness and difficulty sitting still affecting your ability to do your job well, or your relationships with people around you? Has it caused you real problems?

Um... yes, I suppose it has. 

It's... well, it's starting to cost me professionally. I've... missed some details in investigations because I can't just sit and review the files properly. And... I guess I've irritated a few clients by being too restless during meetings. 

Also, the junior detectives... they're less willing to debrief with me now. They feel like I... steamroll them, I guess. So, yes. It's causing some issues.

You mentioned you can focus fine on things that interest you. But when you need to do something less exciting—like organizing files, doing paperwork, or following detailed instructions—do you find yourself having trouble keeping your attention on that task, or do you start it and then not finish it?
Um... no, not really. I mean, the paperwork gets done. It's just part of the job. I don't really have a problem finishing it.

When you're at home or at work and you need to pay close attention to something—like reading an important email, following written instructions, or listening to someone explain something complicated—do you find yourself getting distracted, losing track of what you were doing, or missing important details?
Um... no, not really. I mean, I read what I need to read. I don't think I miss things when it's important. If someone's explaining something, I hear them. It's... it's fine.

When you're working on something that requires you to organize your thoughts or plan out steps—like structuring an investigation or organizing a complex project—do you find that harder than it should be, or do you manage that okay?
Um... no. I manage that okay. Planning out an investigation... it's just what I do. I don't really struggle with that part.

When you're working on something that requires sustained mental effort—like reviewing case files in detail, studying for something, or doing complex analysis—do you find your mind wandering, or do you have to push yourself to stay focused, even if you eventually complete the task?
No, not really. If I have to review a file, I just review it. I mean, my mind doesn't wander any more than anyone else's, I guess. I just do the work.

When you're doing something routine or boring—like filing paperwork or sitting through a long meeting—do you ever feel restless or fidgety, like you need to get up and move around, even if you're trying to stay still?

Um... I suppose. If I'm stuck at the computer, just combing through records... I guess my foot bounces under the desk. Or I'll click a pen. I just... shift around a lot. Sometimes enough that I lose my place in what I'm reading. But... yeah, I guess I do that.

inference_history.note: Initial presentation of difficulty sitting still and staying put in structured settings (client interviews, tutoring, book club). Primary consideration is ADHD (F90.9 - Combined type, F90.1 - Predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type) given the motor restlessness and functional impairment in multiple contexts. Differential includes anxiety disorder (F41.1), depressive disorder (F32.9), autism spectrum disorder (F84.0), and other medical/neurological causes (F06.8).
